panels.title: Slowest endpoints (p95)
panels.description: The 95th percentile by route template. This is the panel to open first: it answers 'which page feels slow' directly, and the route label is the answer. The buckets reach five minutes, so a genuinely stuck endpoint reads as its real duration rather than as 'over ten seconds'.

panels.title: Slowest endpoints (p99)
panels.description: The tail. p95 is what most people meet and p99 is what the unluckiest one in a hundred meets - and a p99 far above p95 means the slowness is occasional rather than constant, which points at contention or a cold cache rather than at the query itself.

panels.title: Requests per second, by route
panels.description: What is actually being asked for. A slow endpoint nobody calls is a different problem from a slow endpoint on every page, and this is how to tell them apart before spending an afternoon.

panels.title: Database round trips per request (p95)
panels.description: THE PANEL THAT FINDS AN N+1. A route whose query count rises with the size of its page is asking the database once per row. Latency cannot show this on a small database - twenty-five extra round trips cost forty milliseconds there and minutes in a real deployment - but the count is wrong at any size. Anything above single digits for a listing deserves a look.

panels.title: Database connection pool
panels.description: in_use against max. A pool pinned at max is the difference between 'one endpoint is slow' and 'everything is slow': a request that cannot get a connection waits without doing any work, and that wait is charged to whatever route it happened to be serving - so the route labels above start pointing at victims rather than the cause.

panels.title: Time spent waiting for a connection
panels.description: Seconds per second spent queueing for the pool. Zero is healthy. Anything sustained here means the pool is the bottleneck and no amount of query tuning on the slow route will help until it is raised or the contention is removed.

panels.title: Error rate by route
panels.description: 5xx as a share of each route's traffic. Separate from the latency panels on purpose: a route that fails fast looks healthy on a latency graph, and a route that is slow because it is retrying a failing dependency looks like a slow query until this panel is read beside it.

panels.title: Requests by status class
panels.description: The whole estate's answers. A rise in 4xx without a rise in 5xx is usually authorization or a client that has got ahead of a deployment; a rise in both is the service.

panels.title: Is anything being scraped
panels.description: One per target. A dashboard that has stopped updating looks exactly like a system that has stopped doing anything, and this is what tells those two apart. Zero here means the graphs above are stale, not that the estate is quiet.
